snippet.title: Experience a Week in Ancient Egypt | Day 1: The Farmer
snippet.description:
The year is 1250 BC. Pharaoh Ramesses II rules the most powerful empire on Earth. And every summer, when the Nile floods, his government does something almost no civilization has ever done: it takes hundreds of thousands of farmers off their fields — and turns them into builders.

This is Day 1 of our 7-part series: 7 Days in Ancient Egypt.

Today, you are a farmer. Your fields are underwater. The state has conscripted you to haul mud bricks for the pharaoh's mortuary temple on the west bank of Thebes. You will carry them on a wooden yoke until your shoulders bruise permanently. You will eat gritty bread that slowly grinds your teeth to stumps. Your wife has a disease from the river water that no doctor in 1250 BC can name. And tonight, you will sleep on a rooftop under a sky so full of stars it casts shadows.

This isn't slavery. This is policy.

Using AI trained on archaeological evidence and historical records, we've reconstructed what one day of ordinary life in ancient Egypt actually looked like — not the gold masks, not the pharaohs, but the real Egypt.


🔔 Subscribe so you don't miss Day 2 — the tomb builder in Deir el-Medina, one of the most literate villages in the ancient world.

snippet.title: You Wouldn't Survive 24 Hours Building the Great Pyramid, 2500 BC
snippet.description:
2.3 million blocks. No wheels. No iron tools. One block positioned every four minutes for twenty years. The Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest structure on Earth for 3,800 years, and everything you think you know about who built it is wrong.
 
They were not slaves. Archaeological evidence shows they were paid workers who received medical care, ate better than most Egyptians, and named their work teams "The Friends of Khufu" and "The Drunkards of Menkaure." They were buried with bread and beer at the foot of the pyramid they built — an honor never given to slaves.
 
Arthur Graves takes you through 24 hours on the Giza Plateau in 2500 BC. The copper chisels that go blunt every few minutes. The sledges dragged across wet sand. The spines compressed by years of lifting multi-tonne blocks. And the pyramid that started as a glowing white beacon visible from forty kilometers away.

snippet.title: What Did Philadelphia Look Like in 1776? (AI Reconstruction) 250 Year Anniversary
snippet.description:
What did Philadelphia look like in 1776 — the year America was born? This AI reconstruction takes you inside the largest, richest, and most important city in colonial America during the most consequential year in its history.

Philadelphia in 1776 was bigger than Boston, bigger than New York, and more diverse than any city in the English-speaking world. With 30,000 residents, over 120 taverns, and the longest outdoor market in the colonies, this wasn't a quiet colonial outpost — it was a thriving, cosmopolitan capital where Quakers, German immigrants, enslaved Africans, and revolutionary firebrands lived side by side on William Penn's original grid streets.

While delegates debated treason inside the Pennsylvania State House, ordinary Philadelphians were living their daily lives just blocks away. This is what that city actually looked like — the cobblestone streets, the printing presses, the slave quarters, and the taverns where the Founding Fathers drank madeira after signing the Declaration of Independence.

In this video, we reconstruct colonial Philadelphia using AI visualization based on historical maps, period accounts, and archaeological evidence:

→ William Penn's grid — the first planned city in America, with streets 100 feet wide
→ High Street Market — the longest outdoor market in the colonies, stretching several blocks
→ The printing capital — at least seven newspapers and dozens of print shops, where Thomas Paine's Common Sense sold 500,000 copies in its first year
→ The tavern culture — over 120 licensed drinking establishments for 30,000 people, including the City Tavern where Adams, Jefferson, and Washington gathered after sessions
→ Slavery in the city of freedom — approximately 1,500 enslaved people lived in Philadelphia while delegates signed "all men are created equal"
→ The free Black community — one of the largest in the colonies, building churches, businesses, and institutions
→ The night watch — men walking dark streets calling out the time and weather
→ The British invasion — Philadelphia would be occupied from September 1777 to June 1778

This is not the version of 1776 you learned in school. This is the real Philadelphia — messy, divided, brilliant, and hypocritical. A city inventing democracy while keeping slaves. A city of taverns and printing presses where the most important document in American history was written, debated, and signed.

2026 marks the 250th anniversary of American independence.

snippet.title: What San Francisco Really Looked Like in 1906 (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
Basically, in this video, I use AI to "resurrect" San Francisco and walk its streets exactly as they were on the morning of April 18th, 1906 — the richest young city in America, just hours before it was lost. It's not just about looking at buildings; we explore the Palace Hotel, the wooden palaces of Nob Hill, the towering Call Building and the lantern-lit alleys of Chinatown at their absolute peak, contrasting that vibrant reality — the "Paris of the West," a city of wood and gold raised in a single lifetime — with the smoking ruins that remained just three days later.

We also break down the cruelest twist of the whole disaster: how a city completely ringed by water burned to the ground because it had nothing left to drink. From the fire chief who predicted the catastrophe and was struck down in its very first minute, to the water mains snapping in three hundred places, the dynamited mansions of Van Ness, and the single gold-painted hydrant that saved an entire neighborhood — it's crazy to see how the city the gold built vanished in just three days.

snippet.title: The Disgusting Truth About Royal Life at Versailles (1685)
snippet.description:
What was daily life actually like inside the Palace of Versailles at the peak of Louis XIV's reign in 1685?

In the year 1685, ten thousand people crammed inside the most magnificent palace in Europe every single day — and fewer than a dozen functional toilets between them. The Sun King relieved himself on a velvet-padded chamber pot in front of a hundred nobles every morning, and being invited to watch was the highest civic honour a French aristocrat could receive. Bathing was considered scientifically lethal. Louis XIV bathed his entire body, by the most generous estimate, three times in his 76-year life.

snippet.title: Experience a Week in Ancient Egypt | Day 6: The Egyptian Doctor
snippet.description:
Three thousand years before Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin, an Egyptian doctor was already prescribing moldy bread for infected wounds. And it worked.

This is Day 6 of our 7-part series: Experience a Week in Ancient Egypt.

Today, you are a physician in Thebes, 1250 BC. You trained at the House of Life at Karnak. You own a copy of the Ebers Papyrus — a 44-page medical scroll containing over 700 remedies, written three hundred years before you were born. You treat infected wounds with honey and willow bark. You wash your hands forty times a day. You have been doing this for twenty years.

This morning you will treat a stonemason's infected hand with a remedy that modern medicine would recognize. This afternoon you will spend three hours trying to save a young woman in labour. You will use every technique your training has given you.

It will not be enough.

Egyptian medicine was the most advanced in the ancient world — used by Greek physicians as a reference for centuries. But medicine in 1250 BC has its limits. And a doctor's job has always included sitting with the people who could not be saved.

Using AI trained on the Ebers Papyrus, the Edwin Smith Surgical Papyrus, and thousands of surviving medical records, we've reconstructed what one day as an Egyptian physician actually looked like.

Imagine a village in 1250 BC where almost everyone can read and write, at a time when global literacy hovers around 3%.

This is Day 2 of our 7-part series: 7 Days in Ancient Egypt.

Tucked behind the cliffs that hide the Valley of the Kings, this village of 68 houses produced the men who carved the royal tombs of Ramesses II. They had latrines. They kept legal records. The women could own property, divorce their husbands, and sue in court. And when their grain rations were late, they staged the first recorded labor strike in human history.

You will chisel the face of Anubis into solid stone by oil-lamp light, eat honey on fresh cheese for breakfast, and walk home at sunset along a cliff path overlooking all of Thebes. Your wife is keeping books in her own name. Your son is faster at reading than you were at his age.

Using AI trained on archaeological evidence and tens of thousands of surviving ostraca — pottery fragments used as scrap paper — we've reconstructed what one day of life in this remarkable village actually looked like.

This AI-generated documentary reconstructs the entire fifty-three day siege of Constantinople — from the arrival of the largest cannon ever built to the final night when Constantine rode through his dying city for the last time. Watch the Theodosian Walls shatter under bombardment, seventy Ottoman warships dragged overland into the Golden Horn, and the desperate last stand at the Mesoteichion breach where the Roman Empire breathed its last.

Every scene in this documentary has been reconstructed using AI video generation, bringing fifteenth-century Constantinople back to life — the Hagia Sophia in its Byzantine glory, the triple walls that held for a thousand years, the legendary Greek Fire, and the moment the last Emperor charged into the enemy and was never seen again.

The fall of Constantinople didn't just end an empire. It ended the Middle Ages, scattered ancient Greek and Roman knowledge across Europe, ignited the Renaissance, and pushed explorers like Columbus to search for new routes to Asia. One night in 1453 changed the course of human history.

snippet.title: You Wouldn't Survive 24 Hours in Ancient Egypt, 1250 BC | AI Reconstruction

No running water. No sewage. Scorpions in the houses. And the first recorded labor strike in history when the government forgot to pay them.
 
This is the real Egypt — with paid sick leave, love poems on broken pottery, and a scorpion charmer on permanent staff.

snippet.title: How Pirates Survived Freezing Nights at Sea Without Heating in 1715
snippet.description:
What was life on a pirate ship really like in 1715? Forty-seven pirates aboard a wooden vessel in the freezing North Atlantic faced a problem nobody talks about in the legends of the Golden Age of Piracy — they could not light a fire. Not a brazier, not a stove, not even a candle past sundown. A single spark in the orlop deck could burn the entire ship to the waterline, and on the open ocean there was no rescue, no land, no second chance. So how did real pirates survive freezing nights at sea without any heating?
In this AI historical reconstruction, we rebuild a single night below decks on a Golden Age pirate ship — the cramped hammocks, the single guttering oil lamp, the layered wool clothing, the forgotten body-heat rituals, and the brutal shipboard rules that kept the wooden hull from becoming a coffin. This is the maritime history of real pirate life — not the rum, not the parrots, not the Captain Jack fantasy. This is what survival actually looked like on a wooden ship in the Age of Sail when the temperature dropped and the wind tore through the rigging for nights on end.
If you enjoy historical reconstructions that show you how people actually lived in the past, subscribe to Worlds Before Us for more cinematic deep-dives into the forgotten realities of history.

🎬 HOW WE BUILT THIS VIDEO — AI HISTORICAL RECONSTRUCTION
At Worlds Before Us, we use a combination of academic historical research and modern AI image and video generation tools to visually reconstruct lives that no camera was ever there to capture. Every frame in this video was generated from period-accurate references — 18th-century shipwright records, surviving sailor clothing, contemporary paintings of ship interiors, and primary-source descriptions of below-deck conditions — and then composed into cinematic sequences. The result lets you see, not just hear, what survival actually looked like on a freezing pirate ship in 1715. We do not invent — we reconstruct, frame by frame, from the historical record.

📚 HISTORICAL SOURCES USED FOR THIS SCRIPT
The script for this video draws on the following published works and primary sources for its claims about Golden Age pirate life, shipboard conditions, fire restrictions, and cold-weather survival:
• David Cordingly — Under the Black Flag: The Romance and the Reality of Life Among the Pirates (Random House, 1995). The standard work on separating pirate myth from documented reality.
• Marcus Rediker — Villains of All Nations: Atlantic Pirates in the Golden Age (Beacon Press, 2004). Academic history of the 1716–1726 Golden Age pirates, including crew sizes, articles, and conditions.
• Marcus Rediker — Between the Devil and the Deep Blue Sea: Merchant Seamen, Pirates, and the Anglo-American Maritime World, 1700–1750 (Cambridge University Press, 1987). Definitive source on daily life aboard early-18th-century Atlantic ships, including sleeping arrangements, watch rotations, and cold-weather practices.
• Colin Woodard — The Republic of Pirates: Being the True and Surprising Story of the Caribbean Pirates and the Man Who Brought Them Down (Harcourt, 2007). Narrative history of the Nassau-based pirate republic.
• Peter Earle — Sailors: English Merchant Seamen 1650–1775 (Methuen, 1998) and The Pirate Wars (Methuen, 2003). Source for shipboard fire regulations, galley use, and the structural reasons no open flame was permitted below decks at night.
• Captain Charles Johnson — A General History of the Robberies and Murders of the Most Notorious Pyrates (T. Warner, 1724). Contemporaneous account written within a decade of the events depicted.
• William Dampier — A New Voyage Round the World (1697). First-hand period account of conditions aboard late-17th and early-18th century ships in cold Atlantic latitudes.
• Royal Museums Greenwich and the National Maritime Museum, London — collections and digitized archives of period sailor clothing, hammock construction, ship-board lighting fixtures, and surviving 18th-century shipwright plans.

snippet.title: Salamis — How 371 Greek Ships Broke a 1,200 Ship Persian Invasion
snippet.description:
In September 480 BC, the Persian Empire put 1,200 warships into a narrow channel of water and lost them in a single afternoon — to a Greek fleet of 371. Five months later, the largest invasion the ancient world had ever assembled was retreating across a frozen river, half its men dead.

This is the battle that ended Persian westward expansion. Not Marathon ten years earlier. Marathon was the warning. Salamis was the answer. The moment the largest empire in the ancient world learned the limit of what could be taken by force.

The numbers tell only part of the story. Persia outnumbered Greece in ships, men, gold, and experienced commanders. In a strait one nautical mile wide, none of that mattered. Only geometry mattered. And one Athenian general — Themistocles — understood the geometry in a way the Persian king did not.

This episode breaks down the battle tactically: the silver strike at Laurion that built the Athenian fleet, the evacuation of Athens, the deception Themistocles sent to Xerxes the night before, the moment the Greek line reversed and rammed. And it places Salamis in the larger Persian arc — the empirical proof of what Cyrus understood and Xerxes forgot.
